title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). The experiment used a shared‑initial generation: baseline and guarded conditions reused the same generated candidate; the guarded pipeline could invoke repair only when the deterministic validator failed (maximum one repair call per task). Provider accounting shows 300 shared initial generation calls and exactly one repair invocation (total model calls used = 301; execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). Results: baseline 299/300 passes, guarded 300/300 passes; contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered hypothesis that GVR produces a materially higher pass rate (target effect 0.10 with ≈80% power) was not supported. We analyse causes (near‑ceiling baseline, minimal repair engagement), provide concrete artifact‑grounded benchmark recommendations, and list reproducibility artifacts and guidance. All preregistration, execution manifest, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived for community reuse.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks (intent→configuration translation, change planning, automated remediation). Prior studies show that out‑of‑the‑box LLMs often produce syntax, topology, or semantic errors; combining generation with deterministic verification and localized repair has been proposed to reduce misconfigurations. However, the community lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that couple intent tasks, explicit validator semantics, and sealed preregistration for confirmatory evaluation of defended pipelines. This paper reports study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1: a preregistered, sealed experiment that (1) constructs a synthetic intent→configuration task bank, (2) implements a deterministic snapshot validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) that enforces explicit intent constraints and required sequences, and (3) runs a paired comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline against a frozen single‑pass generator (declared model gpt-5-mini). Crucially, the design used a shared‑initial generation so the baseline single‑pass output equals the guarded pipeline's initial candidate; the guarded condition could then exercise at most one repair call per failed validator verdict. Our primary confirmatory question: under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per task), does GVR materially increase the per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM?
sections.related_work: Surveys and focused technical reports document rapid growth in LLM applications for network management and explore challenges of hallucination, prompt injection, and verification. Prior empirical work shows LLMs can draft configurations but require verifier assistance or human adjudication to reach operational correctness; generate–validate–repair styles and tool‑assisted prompting have produced improved correctness in limited studies. Other work addresses intent parsing and in‑context learning for configuration translation. Security analyses document prompt‑injection and adversarial attacks that threaten automated NetOps. The literature motivates standardized benchmarks that (a) capture operational task structure, (b) support deterministic machine checking, and (c) allow confirmatory comparisons of defended architectures. Our work contributes a sealed, machine‑checkable benchmark and an archived confirmatory run that exercises these ingredients.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and objectives. We preregistered study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 prior to execution. Primary hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration (artifact archived) defines the task bank, validator semantics, model/configuration settings, exclusion rules, missingness treatments, and the exact analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1).

Task bank and semantics. The deterministic task generator produced 300 synthetic tasks partitioned into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies, and a required_sequence of field changes that must be present in a correct candidate. Tasks span device counts 3–50 and abstract multi‑vendor device models. Tasks are synthetic and contain no private customer data.

Validator and scoring. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implements the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation. The validator performs snapshot, stateless checks: it parses candidate commands, enforces required sequences and workflow_policies, compares final_state to expected_final_state, enumerates violation codes, and returns a binary pass/fail plus diagnostic trace. The validator is intentionally conservative to produce machine‑checkable binary outcomes suitable for confirmatory inference.

Experimental design and shared‑initial semantics. To isolate repair efficacy, each task produced a single shared initial generation that served as the baseline single‑pass candidate. The guarded GVR condition first ran the validator on that shared candidate and, only if the validator failed, was permitted up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Planned_episode_count was 600 (300 shared initial + up to 300 repair calls). The design constrains variance from generation: any guarded improvement must derive from repair rather than a different initial sample.

Model and runtime configuration. The run declared the model requested_model = "gpt-5-mini" and used the hosted adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Recorded adapter/model settings (execution/model_configuration.json, SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) were: provider = "openai_responses"; max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null. The hosted adapter operated in a deterministic sampling mode under the provider semantics recorded in the per‑call traces; in practice, reproducing identical outputs requires replaying the provider call traces and the model_configuration artifact (see Reproducibility below).

Analysis plan. The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed on N=300 paired binary outcomes. The preregistered test was exact McNemar two‑sided; we also computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Sensitivity analyses for missingness and exclusion rules were preregistered; no pairs were excluded and no model calls failed in the run.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and provider audit. Execution completed per preregistration: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, complete_pair_count = 300, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 301. Provider_call_audit recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}. The entire raw results file execution/raw_results.jsonl has SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d; the per‑call provider traces and the single repair provider call are indexed inside that raw_results file and in the execution manifest. The model configuration artifact execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820; the immutable initial master prompt reference provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts: baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table (guarded vs baseline) is: n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. These counts and the analysis artifacts are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55; analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 55eacb88c64f29dc9c5ce1ca7079eca9b4a94b5d3a2970dae019a81a1decf73b).

Discordant episode and repair trace archival. The run invoked the repair stage exactly once; the single repair provider call and the corresponding per‑task manifest entry (the one discordant pair where the baseline failed but the guarded outcome passed) are archived and indexed in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) and in the execution manifest. Auditors can extract the exact per‑episode identifier and the standalone provider_call artifact for the repair invocation by parsing execution/raw_results.jsonl or by consulting the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json in the artifact bundle). The public manuscript quotes the authoritative container‑level SHA of the raw results file above to enable artifact verification; per‑item identifiers are intentionally stored in the archived manifest to preserve machine‑readable traceability.

Representative examples. The archived bundle includes representative per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json … task-000006-*.json). These JSONs show validator traces (normalized_configuration, required_command_count, final_state) and illustrate multi‑step workflows such as shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, and paired_link_atomic_mtu_change. Representative response files (execution/responses/*.txt) and shared initial provider traces are also archived.

Power and sensitivity post‑hoc. The preregistered power routine targeted detection of a 0.10 paired improvement at ≈80% power with N=300 under conservative discordance assumptions. Observed baseline ≈0.997 violates those assumptions: the maximum achievable paired improvement given the observed margins is 0.00333. Therefore the null confirmatory result is explained by arithmetic sensitivity and by near‑complete baseline success rather than by a demonstrable deficiency in analysis execution.
sections.discussion:
Null result interpretation and ceiling effect. The confirmatory null outcome should be read as null for the specific preregistered question under the chosen task bank, deterministic snapshot validator, and constrained repair budget. Two linked instrumental causes produced this outcome: (1) the shared initial generator under deterministic sampling produced correct candidates in 299/300 tasks (near ceiling), and (2) the guarded pipeline's trigger policy limited repair attempts to validator failures and allowed at most a single repair call per task; with so few failures the repair subsystem had almost no opportunity to demonstrate benefit. The single discordant pair (n10=1) sufficed to move guarded from 299→300 passes but is insufficient evidence for the preregistered target effect.

Concrete benchmark and experimental recommendations. Artifact‑grounded lessons produce actionable guidance for future benchmark design where the research goal is to evaluate repair value: (A) increase task difficulty and include adversarial seeding to generate more initial generator failures; (B) permit iterative or larger repair budgets per failed candidate so repairs can iteratively converge; (C) evaluate multiple independent generations per task as baseline samples rather than a single shared candidate to quantify generator variance and selection value; (D) adopt stateful or execution‑emulation validators that model temporal side effects and ordering to expose temporal failure modes; (E) include explicit adversarial prompt/test cases to exercise prompt‑injection and hallucination defenses. Each recommendation directly follows from execution accounting (300 shared initial generations, repair invoked only once) and the per‑task diagnostics archived in the execution bundle.

Reproducibility guidance. The run used deterministic sampling semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = a40e96e2...). In practice, bit‑for‑bit reproduction requires: (1) access to the same provider model release and the same provider invocation semantics; (2) replay of the archived per‑call provider traces found in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...); and (3) use of the same adapter orchestration (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) with the same deterministic sampling setting. We do not publish external provider credentials; instead we publish the full execution bundle (raw_results, provider traces, model_configuration, task_manifest, validator artifacts) so reproductions can verify analysis artifacts and re‑execute only those stages that depend on local provider access.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared‑initial design controls generator variance but focuses the study on repair efficacy when initial candidates are identical; results do not measure gains from guardeds using different initial samples. Construct validity: the deterministic validator enforces snapshot constraints and omits in‑flight temporal execution modeling and vendor CLI idiosyncrasies. External validity: tasks are synthetic (3–50 devices, abstracted vendors) and only one declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one deterministic validator were evaluated. Conclusion validity: the near‑ceiling baseline produces low discordance and thus low statistical power to detect large preregistered effects; exploration and subgroup analyses are underpowered given n10=1.

Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners considering GVR pipelines, our run suggests that for tasks where a deterministic, repeatable generator yields near‑perfect candidates, guarded repair adds little marginal benefit under a constrained repair budget. Conversely, when initial generator quality is lower or adversarial/complex temporal constraints exist, GVR with iterative repairs and stronger validators is more likely to demonstrate value. Our archived artifacts enable communities to instantiate those harder settings without re‑building base infrastructure.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially improves pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported for this task set. Provider accounting shows the guarded repair stage executed only once (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so guarded rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts so the community can extend the benchmark with harder tasks, iterative repair budgets, multi‑generation baselines, and multi‑model comparisons to better evaluate when generate–validate–repair pipelines provide measurable operational value.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the per‑call provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...).

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle (execution manifest and execution/raw_results.jsonl) and are authoritative for auditors.
